person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: method
span.quote: The results provide a model for other institutions for a variety of disciplines to reinforce outcomes through strategic use of the technology.

span.label: virtual reality in art history teaching
span.quote: This study seeks to determine the expectations and results of integrating virtual reality into coursework with students and faculty in Art History.

span.label: practice-report
span.quote: The study surveyed students, first to ascertain the prevalence and familiarity of immersive reality technologies, as well as the perceived benefit of integration into curriculum.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Cheaper head-mounted displays with audio-visual immersivity plus a growing library of educational applications remove the cost and usability barriers, which is what now permits adoption in universities rather than only in the military and medicine.
span.quote: The advances made in Head-Mounted-Displays (HMDs) that allows for both audio and visual immersivity and expanding libraries of educational applications, coupled with a lower price point, have removed many barriers that had previously prevented widespread adoption in academia (Bekele & Champion, 2019).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Prior everyday exposure to consumer motion-sensing and touchscreen devices lowers the perceived novelty of VR, which reduces visitors' reluctance to try immersive installations.
span.quote: Familiarity with similar technology made the public less hesitant to try VR installations.

span.label: What the study measures is what students and faculty say on a rating scale, not any learning outcome.
span.quote: Results were measured via a Likert scale for both faculty and students

span.label: Half the surveyed students did not want the technology used in their other courses.
span.quote: At the same time, only half of the polled group stated that they would like to see such experiences integrated into other coursework

span.label: What the existing literature covers is attributed to what was affordable, not to what was found.
span.quote: The limitations of available scholarship and range of studies can be attributed to the budgetary and technological constraints faced by previous educators

span.label: The field is stated to have limited understanding of how the technology affects any specific learning outcome.
span.quote: However, there is a limited understanding of exactly how VR can be used to enhance specific learning outcomes

span.label: virtual reality
span.quote: little support has been provided by way of examples, resources, and the like to assist faculty in adopting new technologies such as Virtual Reality

span.label: immersive realities
span.quote: Immersive realities (IR) have been radically transforming the delivery of educational materials

span.label: perceived usefulness
span.quote: and perceived usefulness of VR technology compared to other media

span.label: Likert scale
span.quote: Results were measured via a Likert scale for both faculty and students

span.label: learning outcomes
span.quote: However, there is a limited understanding of exactly how VR can be used to enhance specific learning outcomes

span.label: educational benefit - AS PERCEIVED USEFULNESS: what the surveys collect is how useful students and faculty judge the technology to be compared with other media, which is the quantity every result in this paper is about
span.quote: as well as familiarity with technology in general, potential complications with use, the type of experience, and perceived usefulness of VR technology compared to other media

span.label: adoption - DRIVEN BY HARDWARE COST AND AVAILABILITY, not by evidence of effect: the paper traces both the field's slow uptake and the shape of its literature to budget and equipment
span.quote: The potential benefits of integrating immersive realities into traditional humanities curricula have been touted over the last two decades, but budgetary and technical constraints of implementation have limited its adoption

span.label: resistance to a new teaching technology - AS A RECURRING PATTERN, not a fact about VR: the chalkboard after 1801 and the magic lantern in the nineteenth century met the same reaction
span.quote: The introduction of the chalkboard into classes after 1801 was met with widespread revolt from students who had been trained to memorize instead of writing out (Krause, 2001); the adoption of the magic lantern in universities in the nineteenth century, replacing engraved works of art, was slow due to its perceived use primarily as a device for entertainment

span.label: replicates → prior VR-in-education studies (Apostolellis & Bowman, 2014; Cheung et al. 2013; Huang, Rauch & Liaw, 2010; Rizzo et al. 2006; Hussein & Nätterdal, 2015)
span.quote: The results of the study confirm the findings of previous studies, especially the positive correlation between the use of the immersive technology and increased enjoyment of learning (Apostolellis & Bowman, 2014; Ferracani, Pezzatini & Del Bimbo, 2014), motivation (Cheung et al. 2013; Jacobson et al. 2005; Sharma, Agada & Ruffin 2013; Brownridge, 2020), deeper learning and long-term retention (Huang, Rauch & Liaw, 2010; Rizzo, Bowerly, Buckwalter, Klimchuk, Mitura, & Parsons, 2006; Hussein & Nätterdal, 2015).

span.label: perceived usefulness —operationalised-as→ Likert scale
span.quote: The student survey tool used sought to gather demographic information, including first-generation status, age, gender, race and ethnicity, and major, as well as familiarity with technology in general, potential complications with use, the type of experience, and perceived usefulness of VR technology compared to other media. The faculty survey tool likewise collected demographic information, including race and ethnicity, gender, age, and familiarity with technology in general, potential complications with use, and likelihood of adopting for their fields. Results were measured via a Likert scale for both faculty and students

span.label: Likert scale
span.quote: Results were measured via a Likert scale for both faculty and students.

span.label: Roughly three quarters of the surveyed students said the VR assignment helped them learn, and only three of the twenty-three disagreed.
span.quote: 74% of students felt that VR assisted in their learning, while only 3 (12%) of the 23 participants disagreed with its usefulness.

span.label: Three quarters of students judged the VR experience more useful for learning the assigned topic than reading about it.
span.quote: 75% of the participants found that it was more useful to learn about the assigned topic through a VR experience than by reading about it.

span.label: Every faculty respondent judged classroom use of VR to be moderately to extremely useful for their own field.
span.quote: The crucial insight this survey provided is that all respondents stated that using VR technology in their classroom would be moderately to extremely useful.

span.label: The bottleneck reported by faculty was content, not hardware: all but one found it neutral to extremely difficult to locate applications relevant to their discipline.
span.quote: The difficulty, however, is that aside from one participant, all faculty members either reported that finding relevant applications for their field was neutral, or somewhat or extremely difficult.

span.label: Seven of the eight faculty rated the Oculus Quest 2 headset extremely easy to use, indicating a minimal start-up learning curve for instructors.
span.quote: Of the 8 faculty respondents, 7 indicated that using the Oculus Quest 2 headset was extremely easy.

span.label: The preliminary survey showed students are aware of VR but inexperienced with it, already own the phones or tablets needed to run it, want it in their education for career reasons, yet will not spend their own money on a headset.
span.quote: The results of the initial survey confirm that students: are familiar with the technology, though have not experienced it; have the necessary hardware to adapt to using without significant investment; want to see it in their education and understand the importance for their future professions, but are generally unwilling to invest their own resources into acquiring stand-alone hardware themselves.

span.label: Student enthusiasm was bounded: despite reporting learning benefits, only half wanted VR experiences carried over into their other courses.
span.quote: At the same time, only half of the polled group stated that they would like to see such experiences integrated into other coursework.

span.label: Getting started was not a barrier for students, with 83% rating launching the assigned application neutral or easy.
span.quote: 83% reported that launching the technology or getting started into the assigned application was either neutral or easy.

span.label: virtual reality
span.quote: Virtual reality has many definitions, but for our purposes we will rely on the understanding provided by Pope that it is “an experience that encompasses most of the senses, including sight, hearing, and touch, and represents an alternative to reality” (Pope, 2018).

span.label: digital immigrants
span.quote: At the same time, most faculty are digital immigrants, who learned to adapt to new technologies in adulthood (Prensky, 2001).

span.label: "buy rather than build" strategy
span.quote: Resnick and Morgan (2017) recommend beginning with the “buy rather than build” strategy for institutions, ensuring applications address learning outcomes first before developing original content.

span.label: VR assignment integrated into the course
span.term: VR assignment integrated into the course
span.quote: Following the initial survey, assignments using VR were included in all art history classes and select art and design courses Spring 2021.

span.label: student perception of the usefulness and benefit of the VR activity
span.term: student perception of the usefulness and benefit of the VR activity
span.quote: The most important data gathered from the student surveys regards the students’ perception of usefulness and benefit of VR activities.

span.label: faculty likelihood of adopting VR in their own field
span.term: faculty likelihood of adopting VR in their own field
span.quote: They were likewise surveyed regarding their familiarity with VR technology, potential complications with use, and their likelihood to use this technology in their field.

span.label: student demographics (first-generation status, age, gender, race and ethnicity, major)
span.term: student demographics (first-generation status, age, gender, race and ethnicity, major)
span.quote: Demographic data, including first-generation status, age, gender, race and ethnicity, and major was collected from students.

span.label: 74% / 3 (12%) of 23 — share of students who felt VR assisted their learning versus the number who disagreed
span.quote: 74% of students felt that VR assisted in their learning, while only 3 (12%) of the 23 participants disagreed with its usefulness.

span.label: 75% — share of students finding the VR experience more useful than reading about the topic
span.quote: 75% of the participants found that it was more useful to learn about the assigned topic through a VR experience than by reading about it.

span.label: 65% — share of students who would recommend the VR activity to other students
span.quote: 65% of the students stated that would recommend the activity to other students, and over half of respondents reported that they would like to see this technology used in other courses.

span.label: 46 (35.9%) / 33 (24.7%) of 128 — preliminary-survey respondents who were moderately familiar with VR versus not familiar at all
span.quote: Of the 128 respondents, 46 (35.9%) said that they were moderately familiar with the technology, but 33 (24.7%) said they were not familiar at all.

span.label: 106 of 128 — students who owned no VR headset at all, against small counts owning Cardboard, Rift, PlayStation VR and Quest models
span.quote: students were asked if they currently owned a VR headset, and out of 128, 106 responded that they did not, whereas 10 own Google cardboard, 3 own Oculus Rift, 5 own PlayStation VR, 2 Oculus Quest, and 2 Oculus Quest 2.

span.label: 23 (17 + 6) — students who answered the course survey, split into undergraduates and graduate students
span.quote: Of the 23 student respondents surveyed, 17 were undergraduates and 6 graduate students.

span.label: 78% / 81% — share of the student course-survey sample identifying as female and as white
span.quote: 78% identified as female, 81% identified as white, and only one participant indicated that they were a first-generation student.

span.label: 12 — faculty representatives targeted for the faculty survey, two from each school across the university
span.quote: Two faculty representatives from each school (totaling 12) across the University were surveyed for this same period.
